name: Xor Tree
description: For a given sequence of distinct non-negative integers $$$(b_1, b_2, \dots, b_k)$$$ we determine if it is good in the following way: Consider a graph on $$$k$$$ nodes, with numbers from $$$b_1$$$ to $$$b_k$$$ written on them. For every $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$k$$$: find such $$$j$$$ ($$$1 \le j \le k$$$, $$$j\neq i$$$), for which $$$(b_i \oplus b_j)$$$ is the smallest among all such $$$j$$$, where $$$\oplus$$$ denotes the operation of bitwise XOR ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitwise_operation#XOR ). Next, draw an undirected edge between vertices with numbers $$$b_i$$$ and $$$b_j$$$ in this graph. We say that the sequence is good if and only if the resulting graph forms a tree (is connected and doesn't have any simple cycles). It is possible that for some numbers $$$b_i$$$ and $$$b_j$$$, you will try to add the edge between them twice. Nevertheless, you will add this edge only once. You can find an example below (the picture corresponding to the first test case). Sequence $$$(0, 1, 5, 2, 6)$$$ is not good as we cannot reach $$$1$$$ from $$$5$$$. However, sequence $$$(0, 1, 5, 2)$$$ is good. You are given a sequence $$$(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n)$$$ of distinct non-negative integers. You would like to remove some of the elements (possibly none) to make the remaining sequence good. What is the minimum possible number of removals required to achieve this goal? It can be shown that for any sequence, we can remove some number of elements, leaving at least $$$2$$$, so that the remaining sequence is good.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 200,000$$$) — length of the sequence. The second line contains $$$n$$$ distinct non-negative integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$0 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$) — the elements of the sequence.
output_specification: You should output exactly one integer — the minimum possible number of elements to remove in order to make the remaining sequence good.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1446C — Xor Tree [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
